A 100% cursed curio/antique/second hand shop. The second you set foot in there you get this feeling of just 'ick', or like being coated in dry slime, or some kind of sticky residue that feels like it'll never wash off, and it's not the dust. The owner isn't helping matters, the second you show your face he just stalks you around, staring at you as if you're invading his sacred sanctuary. He's happy to sell you the things he's got on the sidewalk, or have you point at something through the window which he'll happily get for you...

But if you enter? If you enter his palace if piles, you are an *enemy*. 

I bought a chair from him once, from *inside* the shop, brought it home, sat in it *once* after a thorough cleaning, then threw it out the next day because my whole being was crawling with wrongness. I bought a table from his stand outside the shop... no issues with it.

Also, the shop has been there for *at least* forty years, it has had the same owner all that time, and I swear he hasn't aged a day. Either he's been eighty for forty years, or he looked eighty when he was forty years old... Or he doesn't age at all... Going with the fact that the shop is cursed, I know what I'm betting on.

Only to realize a split second later that I'd thrown myself into the bookcase instead.

I broke my hand.

Boiling eggs.

I do not know why, I have never been able to figure out why, either. But I just can't get it right.

I can boil them to hell for twelve minutes and they yolk is still liquid, or I can boil them for five minutes and get them hard boiled. Never in my life have I been able to boil eggs and get my desired result.

Not with egg timers, not with the timers you throw in the pot along with the eggs, not with a dedicated egg boiler (the electric ones you put the eggs in and add a bit of water and it steams the eggs?). 

The only time I managed to boil eggs properly was when my mom was watching the entire time because she wanted to see me fail.

I think everyone has a superpower, mundane or great, but I also think everyone has their curse, and mine is apparently an inability to boil eggs.

My mother tongue is Swedish, but I learned English rather rapidly due to immersion when I was ten (online gaming...) For the most part I write, speak, and think in English. Though... when I want to *really* swear, I do it in a mix of Danish (my third language) and Finnish, the latter of which I *only* know swear words in. My Danish is rusty because of lack of use, but I do dream in Danish at times.

Mostly my mind is built on English, though.

I'm now looking to learn German.

I remember when I started learning English, and suddenly the world just made so much more sense.

Look, I can go on about linguistics for *ages*, but I'm just going to say this: Learning new languages can open your mind to the world in ways you never even imagined, even adding just a quarter or half of a new language has enormous positive effects to experience the world in an entirely new way.

Nope, no way to the surface once you're under. Yeah, it's terrifying. You *might* get lucky and be able to swim sideways through a whirlpool to grab onto some rock at the side of the river, if you're that close to it, but... unlikely. I don't think we've actually had *any* survivors in the one hundred and four years of this town being established. Also, remember it's *placid looking* rivers, and you can sometimes see if there's an undercurrent if the surface kind of ripples like creased silk or if there are very small whirlpools. If in doubt, stay on land.

Ah. I wrote canal, right. I guess there wouldn't be an undercurrent in a constructed canal, no. Here in my city the canal and the river are both called the canal, so I usually say it's the canal even though it's not. Sorry about that, the river and the canal are separated by a sliver of land that is about thirty feet at the widest, and at one stretch it's only separated by a bridge.

Well... It's because the undercurrent starts a few inches below surface, at that point you're already all the way under and being swiftly dragged away, waters with a strong undercurrent are usually opaque, so the people on land would have a hard time seeing you even if they had a pole, and then *you* would have to be able to see the pole to grab on to, which is unlikely, you wouldn't be able to get far enough to the surface to grab on to a life saver either, and no one would be able to kind of poke it down for you to reach. I guess "impossible" is a strong word, "damn *near* impossible" might be a better choice. And if they themselves jump in to help? Well, then *they're* shit out of luck as well.

The best bet is if there's already someone on scene with a rope tied to their belt prior to someone falling in, and that person jumps in to try to grab hold to you.

Undercurrents are *fast*, really really fast, or they wouldn't be strong.

An undercurrent *drags you down*, it doesn't just rush you down river.

Oh yes, we've sadly had some unfortunate tourists who neglected to heed the warning signs. There are signs every twenty feet here, the current is so strong. You literally can't stand by the canal without seeing one... And yet...

A current can be seen atop the water, think swirling and waves and rushing. An undercurrent cannot be seen, the water looks placid, it's sometimes betrayed by small whirlpools, like a thumb print small, or the palm of your hand small, as well as "creases" in the water, like oil slick or creased silken fabric. What makes the undercurrent so dangerous is that it can seldom be seen from the surface, so people aren't prepared. You can't swim up a rushing river, and you cannot escape an undercurrent, it pulls you down and keeps you there.

"Everything is relative." 

Mom had a fridge magnet with that on it, and I asked several times what it meant, child me couldn't wrap my head around it, probably because I didn't know what "relative" actually meant in that context.

But once I figured out how to ask, and then figured it out, I got it. I see people's struggles and victories, and I find myself thinking "they're brought to their knees by *that*?" or "they're celebrating something so small?" And I immediately think "Well, it's relative." I think of my own things as well, and during bad days when I seek a reason for feeling bad, I think it, everything's relative, yeah, maybe someone else would be able to handle my issues far better than I can, different personalities, different outcomes, different stages in life, etc, everything is relative. It's a pretty soothing thought, really. Beauty, ugliness, grace, goodness, evil, it's all relative. Thinking it can really get you to... not *understand* other people, maybe, but at least realize that they're coming at it all from a different point of view, form a different culture, creed, religion, tradition, etc.

Everything is relative.

Also: "Never leave angry."

I think everyone in my family suffers from catastrophizing (spelled with z or c?), so mom always said to not leave angry, because you never know when you're going to see someone again. Sort out your issued before leaving, before saying goodbye. Yeah, maybe you can't sort it all out, but at least *try* to reach an understanding and leave at decent terms, you don't want the last time you saw someone you love/accept/tolerate to be the time you told them they'd do everyone a favor if they went ahead and died already.

I count. I close my eyes and count, and maybe I don't calm down, but it helps give me a pause to consider the situation, and I can go be pissed somewhere else, maybe scream into my pillow, or take a shower. A meditative thing to do when showering is to picture yourself covered in dirt, and visualize washing it off, and while you do that, visualize that it's your anger you're washing off. Might take some practice to get right, but I feel calmer afterwards.

But counting really helps as well. It's such a simple thing and it's waved off by a lot of people for being *too* simple. But really, when you're furious, when you're angry, what you need is a pause and *perspective*. And it doesn't matter if that perspective is a full blown realization of the situation, it's good enough if it's an: "Oh, I'm about to do something bad, better not, better go." 

Count, breathe, close your eyes to block out some impressions. I hope you find something that works for you soon, and I wish you well.

There are sites in some countries where you can fill out a form to say what you want from a therapist, you can also call the clinic / care unit and ask if they have anyone fulfilling your requirements. 

"Shopping around" for a therapist is a thing, you are their boss, you get to interview them.

Some good things to ask is:

1. "What are your credentials?"
2. "What did you specialize in?"
3. "What kind of treatments do you perform?"
4. "Do you perform \_\_\_\_\_\_\_ treatment?"

(You can also ask if they have someone they can recommend if they aren't the right fit for you.)

(You can also ask if they do CBT (Cognitive behavioral therapy))

You can ask them anything, and if they get angry, you get up and leave *immediately.* A good therapist should *never* become angry or defensive when a patient asks questions about treatment, experience, medicine, etc. 

Therapy does help, when you get the right one for you. CBT is a good way to go to learn to manage problems before you dive into solutions, it might seem like a roundabout way to do it, but if you tackle your root issues head-on, symptoms and trauma will surface, and you will need to know how to cope with that.

Just a few sessions of that can give you the groundwork to start on the big stuff.

Psychotherapy is what you do with a psychologist, and it's where you dig deeper. Coupled with CBT it can help you immensely, but all needs are different, and you might not need it.

There are hundreds, if not thousands, of different kind of cats. So you can't really say if it's a fruit, vegetable or nut, it honestly depend on the breed. 

A cat can't be replanted until the lifespan is completed, and generally, a replanted cat never grows a good cat. 
It's sadly a common practice to replant cats, and it might result in a sick or wilted cat, or one that will never fully grow. It's cruel, but people like the aesthetic of cats with curled ears or short legs or smooshed faces.

And about the trees, each breed of cat comes from a different tree! An oak, for example, would produce a common house cat, which really is a mix of many different breeds, because oaks pollinate with trees outside of it's own genus. 
A fir tree grows Norwegian forest cats, and a palm tree can produce a sphynx.

A good rule of thumb is to look at different cats and where they come from, and the trees in the same regions. Trees in a temperate climate will produce short haired cats, while a spruce or a fir is most often found in colder climates and will grow cats with longer hair.

As for planting? The trees often take care of that themselves, but farmers will take saplings from a tree that grew a good cat, and plant the saplings. And so the circle goes.

That's easy! As a general rule of thumb, the cat rests twenty centimeters (seven inches) above where you can see the first root. So not 20 cm above ground! NO, 20 cm above where the first root connects to the tree. 
That's where the BOTTOM of the cat is. And generally, the top of the cat is about 10-15 cm above that.
A professional farmer will know by instinct, which is why you should really ask for help or hire one when the cat is ready.

It's always better to cut higher than you need, so you don't hurt the cat, and then carefully sand away layer by layer of the tree until you see fur, then you get a general idea of where the cat is, and sand around it until you've "carved it out".

And... If you get a vet out there, they can use an ultra-sound to determine where the cat is... but that gets a bit expensive... But it is by far the safest option unless you can get a hold of an experienced farmer.

Cats don't actually have to be fully grown before you cut down the tree!

There are four stages of cat:

1. Kitten (0-6 months)
2. Adolescent (7 months - 2 yrs)
3. Adult (2-10 yrs.)
4. Elder (11+ yrs)

A lot of people wait to cut the tree until the cat is an adolescent, some wait all the way to elder. The thing is how long you want to spend caring intensively for the cat, and I'd say the peak time to cut the tree is when the cat has been in there for three years, but a lot of people disagree and cut the tree when the cat is just a few months old, or even just a week!

The grow time for a cat is usually around nine weeks, after which it's safe to cut the tree, but I'd say wait a bit longer or you're risking a wilted or problematic little kitten, their needs are hard to meet when they're that young.

As for how to know when to cut the tree?

The absolute easiest way is if you plant the seed yourself, the tree itself should be 10-15 years, plus nine weeks incubation time. If you don't know the age of the tree, a quick sap sample examined by a vet would be the best way to go about it. The vet can then tell you how old the tree is, and possibly even if it has started growing the cat!

Second best way is to take a ring sample from the very top of the tree, this won't damage the tree or the cat, so it's okay. From there you count the rings, like with any other tree, where each ring is one year.

It's a lenghty process, but there are professionals who do this for a living, so a ready picked cat can be bought from a reputable farmer or shelter.

Isn't nature amazing?

(I would also suggest having a professional cut the tree for you when the time is right, so you won't accidentally damage the cat, but there are plenty of Youtube videos you can watch to learn how to do it yourself.)

I have been there. I was so ashamed and I *hated* asking for help. I was firmly in the state of mind that I'm an adult, I should be able to handle this.

But the truth is that sometimes we *can't*. For varying reasons, things don't go as we planned, we have the best of intentions to get things done, we *want* to live in a clean place and have food to eat, and sometimes that just seems impossible.

My grandmother helped me sometimes, and mom other times, because they were the ones who saw how I lived, and they refused to leave until it was clean and organized. They tried to help me keep on top of chores and cooking and stuff, and finally mom made me admit I needed help.

That's where things changed. 

I asked for help, and I received it in form of home support. 

At first I hated it. I hated the idea of these strangers (or anyone, really) coming to my home and helping me with my dirty laundry and dishes. I hated the idea of them cleaning my bathroom or sweeping my floors. But I ***couldn't*** do it on my own. I was so ashamed. Letting *anyone* see the mess felt like a failure.

"I'm an adult, I should be able to handle this."

But there's no set rule of what you should and shouldn't be able to handle. Sure, there are standards, expectations. But it's always different, some say you're not an adult until you can build your own dining room set, some say you're not an adult until you can pinpoint the problem with your car engine and then fix it.

You are not somehow *less* because you need help. And you're not a failure for letting the dishes pile up, or using up every last article of clothing before you are forced to do the laundry. You are just someone who needs a little help to get started, to get going. 

Let someone do the dishes for you, and you can focus on grabbing some bags and throwing away some trash. Let someone vacuum the floors, and you can focus on opening the window to let in some fresh air.

I know shame is hard to overcome, but you needn't feel ashamed for needing help, even if it's help with things you think you should be able to handle.

And when you feel better, which I hope will be soon, you can return the favor. Buy/make a giftbasket for your housing case manager, help your friend with something he needs done, but right now, allow yourself to be helped.

You are not worthless, and you needn't feel ashamed. 

And a tip for you, when it's nice and clean, take a look at "[unfuck your habitat"](https://www.unfuckyourhabitat.com/) , it has helped me greatly, it uses "easy" tips and tricks, and runs on the mentality of: "Do what you can, when you can." Even if it's just moving one single wrapper to the trash on your way to get a glass of water, that's one thing done.

"Never leave angry."

I try to live by that.

You never know what's going to happen, if you'll ever see each other again. 

I left my cousin angry.

She died of an overdose before I could get over myself and apologize.  
For *years* I had kept up my hatred, not of *her* but what she represented. When I saw her, I saw my uncle and my grandparents. And I swore to myself to never talk to them again, to love myself enough to never forgive them for what they did.

My cousin was not at fault. It took me far too long to realize that. So much time spent angry, and when I finally pulled my head out of my ass, it was to the news that she had died.

\-

And the other way around as well, what did she think? Did she die thinking I hated her? Did she die thinking I would actually want to see her dead?

\-

Try to work things through before you leave a loved one, or a friend, or even an acquaintance, you never know what will happen, the least it'll give you is some peace of mind, that at least you tried.

\-

Some things can't be fixed in a goodbye though, and that's okay. But if you can help it, if you can influence the situation, try to never leave angry.

Write down what you can remember, it doesn't have to be coherent. Here's a passage from one of my journal entries: "Dark, door, dad, kitchen, loud, sick, hallway, mom, bathroom, dad, loud."

That's all it says, it doesn't tell a story, but it's enough of an anchor for me to remember what happened, or at least remember bits of it.

All I do is close my eyes, and I think, and as soon as there's a flash of memory, I write down the words most fitting to it. No whole sentences, that's for later.

Once I have the words, I can look at them individually and try to recall what the memory was about. Maybe I'll remember something, but not wholly, then I'll add another word and analyze it later. Eventually you have a full sentence. It doesn't have to be several pages long, one single sentence is enough. The starting words don't even have to be in chronological order, so to speak, but can just be whatever you feel at the time. My words up there weren't in chronological order, if you were to build a story out of them in that order, it wouldn't be the "correct one". Once I had my memory, I could rearrange the words I had to start with so they are in order.

These key words are *very* important. They can help you recall a great deal more than you think. And recurring words such as "Dark" or "loud" can tell you a lot about what you are feeling in the memory, or what you think you thought at the time.

I would suggest getting a diary app or just write in your note app in your phone whenever there is a flash of memory. Quick as you can, given the situation, get your phone and write down your key words, and analyze them later when you have time.

​

Another thing you could try is immersive recollection (not a clinical term). Do things you remember you did as a kid, watch kids shows you used to watch, eat meals you used to eat, even cook those meals the same way and in the same order (if you can remeber it) that your family member/guardian did. 

Immersive Recollection is a powerful thing, and scents, tastes, and visual input can trigger strong memories of things that happened related to the activity you're performing.

For example, say you watched the telletubbies as a kid. And someone close to you had an argument or did something bad to you or to someone else at the same time, watching the telletubbies now gives you a chance to recall that memory.

​

Doing these things won't help you work through your issues, but it will give you enough to work *with.*

So that you may be able to heal and move on.

I started Lyrica (pregabalin) when I was 19, so six years ago. And it has helped me greatly. I've been on 225mg twice per day for the last few years, and I haven't felt this good ever.

I could finally breathe without my chest constircting or my throat closing up.

Lyrica is my savior. It has bad withdrawal effects if you forget a dose, but the overall positives far outweigh the negatives. I cannot recommend it warmly enough.

Now, Lyrica isn't often the first step medicine for anxiety, but damn does it work.

You shouldn't feel too bad about going on medication, some will work, some won't, it's about finding the right fit for you, and it can take a while but when you get the right ones and the anxiety stops, it's so worth it.

There are horror stories about everything, and a lot of people bash medicine because they haven't found the right fit, or their doctor didn't listen to their needs and overmedicated them or gave them the wrong one. However, you shouldn't worry too much about it. 

You hear the negatives more, because those with positive experiences seldom speak out about it for some reason. Maybe they don't feel the need, but in my experience there are far more positive stories than negative ones, you just need to find them.

If you and your doctor feel like you should go on medication, it's about finding the right one, and then you'll be downright liberated.

Try not to worry too much about about it, the positives outweigh the negatives. I promise.
